Global Health — Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs)

The Epidemiological Transition
1990 → 2024

A structural shift from communicable to chronic disease dominance has reshaped the global burden of illness over three decades, with stark inequalities persisting across income groups.

Communicable & Nutritional
Non-Communicable (NCD)
Injuries

62%
vs. 36% in 1990 — structural reversal
01 — Structural Transition

From Communicable to Chronic: A Burden Reversal

In 1990, communicable diseases accounted for more than half of global DALYs. By 2024, NCDs had become the dominant category, nearly doubling their share as infectious disease burden fell sharply.

1990 — Global DALY Composition
Total: 2,150.3 million DALYs
2024 — Global DALY Composition
Total: 2,408.4 million DALYs
02 — Income Group Disparity

Unequal Transition: Burden Composition by Income Group

Low-income countries retain a high communicable disease share (53% in 2024), while high-income countries are overwhelmingly NCD-dominated (88%). The transition has occurred across all groups, but the gradient remains stark.

Disease Burden Composition by Income Group — 1990 vs 2024
Stacked bar shows percentage share of total DALYs (communicable / NCD / injuries)
03 — Cause Rank Shifts

Changing Hierarchy: Top 10 DALY Causes, 1990 → 2024

Ischemic heart disease rose from rank 4 to rank 1. Lower respiratory infections fell from rank 1 to rank 6. Diabetes mellitus and depressive disorders entered the top 10. Measles and diarrheal diseases fell out entirely.

04 — Cause Magnitude

Top 10 DALY Causes: Absolute Burden Comparison

Ischemic heart disease now carries 192 million DALYs globally—the largest single-cause burden. Diarrheal diseases and measles have dropped out of the top 10, replaced by diabetes, low back pain, and depressive disorders.

Top 10 Causes — DALYs in Millions (1990 vs 2024)
Colored by disease category; causes ranked by 2024 burden

Data: Global Burden of Disease (GBD) methodology. 2024 figures are projected estimates. Communicable category includes maternal, neonatal, and nutritional conditions. Sources: IHME GBD Study 2021 with 2024 projections.
